title: Easy Things Are Easy Hard Things Are Hard
author: Didau, David
summary: Didau contrasts two teaching styles using the metaphor of entertainers: Johnny G (charismatic, low-bar, excitement-focused) versus Janet (calm, focused on meaningful activity like sewing). While excitement is easy, creating focused learning environments where students work hard on important, difficult tasks requires considerable skill and organizational support. New teachers often default to entertainment to manage classroom behavior, but experience and school culture supporting discipline enable them to prioritize deep work. Didau argues that if schools value culturally rich curricula and student mastery, they must support teachers in maintaining order and valuing hard work rather than leaving it to chance.
points: Doing easy things is easy; doing hard things takes enormous effort, especially for new teachers who need determined organizational support.
Charismatic, entertainment-focused teaching (Johnny G) appeals naturally to students but sacrifices deep learning; calm, focused teaching (Janet) requires more skill.
As explicit instruction and knowledge-rich curricula become normal, schools can move away from relying on entertainment-based classroom management.
Teacher development cannot be left to chance or Darwinian competition; schools must systematically support teachers in maintaining discipline and high expectations.
Building norms around hard work and orderly classrooms takes time, experience, and organizational support; without it, talented teachers leave the profession.
quotes: Making five-year-olds squeal with delight by burping doesn't require all that much. Honestly, he'd have been hard pressed not to over-excite them. It struck me that doing things that are easy is, well, easy.
Now, if he'd managed to get them all quiet and concentrating then that really would have been impressive. Going against the grain is always trickier.
It's a lot easier to do what's easy. Doing what's hard—maintaining discipline and insisting on high standards—takes enormous effort and, especially when you're new, determined support.

If we don't want to leave teachers' development to chance, if we value calm, ordered classrooms and students working hard to master a culturally rich curriculum then we must provide the support for teachers to maintain order and to value hard work.” Archived from David Didau on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
